title: L4 moves connections fast; L7 reads the request and routes it
caption: A common stack: a network (L4) LB in front of a fleet of L7 proxies that terminate TLS and route by path.

steps.text: The L4 LB sees only IPs and ports. It picks a proxy per connection and forwards packets without reading them: millions of connections, little CPU.
The L7 proxy terminates TLS and reads the HTTP request: method, path, headers, cookies.
Now it can route by content (/api to one service, /img to another), retry a failed backend, and add auth or headers.

scenarios.name: Backend down
scenarios.summary: Because L7 routes by path, a dead image service only breaks /img: the proxy fails those requests fast and /api keeps working.

steps.text: The image service fails its health checks.
Requests for /img/* get a fast 503 from the proxy (or a placeholder image) instead of hanging.
/api/* is routed as usual: the failure is contained to one route.

scenarios.name: Long-lived connections
scenarios.summary: L4 balances connections, not requests: a few HTTP/2 or WebSocket connections carrying many requests can pin load to one proxy.

steps.text: A mobile app opens one HTTP/2 connection and sends thousands of requests over it for hours.
The L4 LB chose a proxy once, at connect time. Every request on that connection lands on the same proxy, however busy it is.
The L7 proxy balances each request separately across backends, so the services behind it stay even.
Mitigation at L4: cap connection lifetime (servers send GOAWAY) so clients reconnect and get rebalanced.

scenarios.name: Alternative: L4 only
scenarios.summary: Skip the L7 tier: fewer hops and less CPU, but no routing by path, no per-request retries, and every server terminates TLS itself.

steps.text: The L4 LB forwards encrypted TCP streams; it never sees a URL.
Each connection goes to one app server, which decrypts TLS and serves every route.
Trade-off: great for raw TCP, databases or one uniform service. Splitting /api and /img into separate fleets needs an L7 layer again.

scenarios.name: Risk: TLS at the proxy
scenarios.summary: Terminating TLS makes the L7 tier CPU-heavy and a target: scale it horizontally behind L4 and re-encrypt if the network is untrusted.

steps.text: A traffic spike means a flood of new TLS handshakes, the most expensive thing a proxy does.
One overloaded proxy adds latency to every service behind it.
Mitigation: many identical proxies behind the L4 LB, session resumption to skip full handshakes, and autoscaling on CPU.
